questions.question: Explain three preventive network security mechanisms that an organization can deploy, describing how each mechanism protects the network.

marking_points.point: A firewall filters traffic entering and leaving the network according to predefined security rules.
marking_points.quote: Control incoming and outgoing traffic on network with predetermined security policies.

marking_points.point: A proxy server improves data security and network performance by acting as a firewall and web filter, sharing connections and caching data.
marking_points.quote: Proxy servers act as a firewall and web filter, provide shared network connections, and cache data to speed up common requests.

marking_points.point: Network segmentation creates boundaries between segments whose assets share a common function, risk or role.
marking_points.quote: Boundaries between network segments where computing assets within the segment have a common function, risk or role within an organization.

marking_points.point: A remote access VPN gives individual hosts or clients secure access to the organization's network.
marking_points.quote: Provides remote and secure access to an organization network to individual hosts or clients

marking_points.point: Zero Trust Network Access limits each user to only the access and permissions needed for their role.
marking_points.quote: A user should only has access and permission that required to fulfill the role

marking_points.point: IDS/IPS detect or prevent attacks such as brute force, denial-of-service and exploitation of network vulnerabilities.
marking_points.quote: To detect or prevent the network security attacks such as brute force attacks, Denial-of-Service attacks and exploits of network vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Refer to your answer in (a). Explain six (6) facts about the NGSCB/Nexus components, covering the Nexus kernel, the Nexus Computing Agent, and how they relate to the TPM and the operating system.

marking_points.point: Nexus is described as a security kernel that is authenticated on boot.
marking_points.quote: Security kernel, authenticated on boot

marking_points.point: Nexus authenticates trusted programs.
marking_points.quote: Authenticates trusted programs

marking_points.point: Nexus provides the application interface to the TPM.
marking_points.quote: Application interface to TPM

marking_points.point: Nexus does not trust the operating system.
marking_points.quote: Does not trust OS

marking_points.point: The Nexus Computing Agent is a trusted software component.
marking_points.quote: Trusted software component

marking_points.point: The NCA runs in trusted mode and communicates with Nexus.
marking_points.quote: Runs in trusted mode that communicates with Nexus

questions.question: Explain how a substitution cipher works and what serves as its key.

marking_points.point: Encryption replaces each plaintext letter with a different letter to produce the ciphertext.
marking_points.quote: In substitution ciphers, we replace the plain-text letters with other letters

marking_points.point: The substitution rule itself acts as the key of the cipher.
marking_points.quote: The substitution rule is the key

questions.question: State six points about access control structures, covering the access control matrix, access control lists and capability lists, including one advantage and one disadvantage of each structure.

marking_points.point: The access control matrix is described as a basic control structure.
marking_points.quote: ACM is a basic control structure.

marking_points.point: An advantage of the access control matrix is that it is easy to verify.
marking_points.quote:
Advantages:
clarity of deﬁnition
easy to verify

marking_points.point: A disadvantage of the access control matrix is poor scalability.
marking_points.quote:
Disadvantages:
poor scalability
poor handling of changes

marking_points.point: An access control list is an object-centered description of access rights.
marking_points.quote: ACL is an object-centered description of access rights:

marking_points.point: An advantage of ACLs is that object access rights are easy to access.
marking_points.quote:
Advantages:
easy access to object access rights
relative easiness of management using abstractions

marking_points.point: A capability list is a subject-centered description of access rights.
marking_points.quote: C-List is a subject-centered description of access rights:

questions.question: Explain the goals of access control and the role of a reference monitor.

marking_points.point: Access control aims to grant access to subjects.
marking_points.quote: Goals of access control: Granting access

marking_points.point: Access control aims to limit access.
marking_points.quote: Limiting access

questions.question: Describe six (6) techniques used by malware to propagate itself or to hide and maintain control of an infected system.

marking_points.point: A boot sector virus saves the original master boot record in a safe location before overwriting it with an infected version.
marking_points.quote: Save the original MBR in a safe location

marking_points.point: A COM executable virus replaces the program entry point with a jump to the virus body, which later restores the original entry point.
marking_points.quote: Replace a program entry point                                   with a jump to a virus body

marking_points.point: An EXE executable virus overwrites the program header so that the entry point switches to the virus.
marking_points.quote: Over write a program header to switch the entry point to a virus

marking_points.point: A rootkit masks malicious processes and software in the infected system so that privileged remote access is maintained.
marking_points.quote: Rootkits are a type of malware that mask malicious processes and software in the infected systems to ensure privileged remote access.

marking_points.point: A rootkit is usually installed after a vulnerability has been found and detected, keeping the infected computer under the malware author's control.
marking_points.quote: They are usually installed after a vulnerability has been found and detected so that the infected computer continues to be under the control of the malware author.

marking_points.point: Spyware steals user logins and passwords, records sites visited, logs keystrokes and redirects browsers to unwanted sites.
marking_points.quote: They steal user logins and passwords, document sites visited, log keystrokes and even redirect browsers to unwanted sites.

questions.question: Describe the Samy worm as a malware case study, covering how it injected code, how it spread, and its outcome.

marking_points.point: The worm injected JavaScript into a user profile by writing to document.body.innerHTML.
marking_points.quote: Inject Javascript into a user proﬁle using document.body.innerHTML

marking_points.point: It obtained the victim's list of friends (heros) by issuing a GET request on a user profile.
marking_points.quote: Get the list of user’s heros by using a GET on a user proﬁle

marking_points.point: It added Samy as a friend by performing XML-HTTP requests against the addFriends page.
marking_points.quote: Add Samy as a ﬁeld by performing XML-HTTP on the addFriends page

marking_points.point: Any user visiting an infected profile had their own profile and friends list infected, so the worm spread through page visits.
marking_points.quote: Any user who visits an infected user’s page will gets proﬁle infected with Javascript and his friends list infected with Samy

marking_points.point: The worm ultimately infected about 1,000,000 MySpace profiles, showing the large-scale impact of an XSS-based worm.
marking_points.quote: Eventually about 1,000,000 MySpace proﬁles were infected.

marking_points.point: The underlying XSS weakness is that any web application returning user input without filtering is a potential XSS vulnerability.
marking_points.quote: Any web application that returns user input without ﬁltering is a potential XSS vulnerability!

questions.question: Discuss biometric mechanisms and technologies as an alternative to passwords, covering their definition, categories, and the strengths and weaknesses of specific biometric methods.

marking_points.point: A biometric is defined as a physiological or behavioural characteristic of a human that can distinguish one person from another and can theoretically be used for identification or verification.
marking_points.quote: A biometric is a physiological or behavioural characteristic of a human being that can distinguish one person from another and that theoretically can be used for identification or verification of identity.

marking_points.point: Biometric applications are divided into two sectors: psychological (such as iris, fingerprints, hand, retinal and face recognition) and behavioural (such as voice, typing pattern and signature).
marking_points.quote: Biometric applications available today are categorized into 2 sectors

marking_points.point: Retinal scanning is very efficient and cannot be spoofed, but it requires the user to look directly into the reader and raises acceptability concerns such as light exposure and hygiene.
marking_points.quote: Very efficient – cant be spoofed!

marking_points.point: Fingerprint biometrics suffer from disadvantages including racial issues, dirt, grime and wounds, finger placement problems, and the need for liveness detection because they can be spoofed.
marking_points.quote: Can be spoofed – liveness                                              important!

marking_points.point: Iris scanning captures a unique pattern, is coloured and visible from far, requires no touch, and overcomes retinal scanner issues, although contact lenses may be a problem.
marking_points.quote: Scans unique pattern of iris

marking_points.point: Biometric methods are one of the alternative user authentication mechanisms, alongside smart cards and two-factor authentication, to the common but insufficiently secure password.
marking_points.quote: Alternative user authentication mechanisms are smart cards, biometric methods and two-factor authentication.

questions.question: State six facts about Kerberos and single sign-on as authentication mechanisms, covering their motivation, design criteria, login process and limitations.

marking_points.point: Single sign-on reduces the need for users to memorize passwords.
marking_points.quote: Reduce the need to memorize passwords

marking_points.point: Single sign-on reduces the time users spend typing passwords.
marking_points.quote: Reduce the time spent on typing passwords

marking_points.point: Kerberos is designed to be secure against eavesdropping by never transmitting passwords in clear text.
marking_points.quote: Security against eavesdropping: no                                       password transmission in clear text.

marking_points.point: Kerberos is designed for transparency, so the user is unaware of any authentication beyond the initial login.
marking_points.quote: Transparency: user is not aware of any                            authentication beyond an initial login.

marking_points.point: During Kerberos login, the hash of the user's password becomes the secret key of the client or user.
marking_points.quote: The hash value of his password                                                      KU = h(P) becomes a secret key of the                                                  client/user.

marking_points.point: A limitation of Kerberos is that it is relatively complex to install.
marking_points.quote: Relatively complex in installation.

questions.question: Explain the distinction between a vulnerability, a threat and an attack, and state three countermeasure activities that together protect assets against threats.

marking_points.point: A vulnerability is a weakness in a system that can be exploited to cause damage to assets.
marking_points.quote: Vulnerabilities: Weakness of a system that can be exploited to damage assets

marking_points.point: A threat is only a potential violation of security, not an actual one.
marking_points.quote: Threats: A threat is a                                                          “potential” violation of                                                                    security

marking_points.point: An attack is the actual violation of security that has occurred.
marking_points.quote: Attacks: The actual                                                                               violation of security

marking_points.point: A threat is an entity that represents a constant danger to an asset.
marking_points.quote: Threat: object, person, or other entity representing a constant danger to an asset

marking_points.point: An attack is a deliberate act that exploits a vulnerability.
marking_points.quote: Attack: a deliberate act that exploits vulnerability

marking_points.point: Protecting assets requires combining prevention, detection and response techniques as countermeasures.
marking_points.quote: Protection of assets encompasses prevention, detection and response techniques

questions.question: Explain five points about the security mechanisms built into Windows, covering the directory service used to organise resources, the registry hives that hold security data, how access rights are encoded, and why the complexity of these mechanisms can itself be a risk.

marking_points.point: Active Directory, introduced in Windows 2000, is an LDAP-like directory service used to organise system resources such as users and groups, security credentials and certificates, and security policies.
marking_points.quote: Active directory introduced in Windows 2000 is an LDAP-like directory service for organization of system resources:

marking_points.point: The registry is a hierarchical database holding critical system information, and its security-related hives include SAM (the SAM database) and Security (security logs).
marking_points.quote: A hierarchical database containing critical system information

marking_points.point: Access rights describe what one can do to an object and are encoded as a 32-bit mask, with standard rights such as DELETE and WRITE_DAC common to most object types.
marking_points.quote: Describe what one can do to an object

marking_points.point: Windows contains complex mechanisms for user account and object management and access control, and DACS allow fine-grained access control of heterogeneous entities.
marking_points.quote: Windows systems contain complex security mechanisms for user account and object management as well as access control.

marking_points.point: The complexity of Windows security mechanisms is also its enemy, because misconfiguration as well as implementation bugs may lead to severe security incidents.
marking_points.quote: The complexity of Windows security mechanisms is also its enemy: misconﬁguration as well as implementation bugs may lead to severe security incidents.
